data.title: Ahead of Schedule: Meta’s Early Earnings Shift Driven by Muse AI Enthusiasm
data.description:
• Meta moved its Q3 report to October 21, a full week earlier than expected, a historically bullish move backed by surging enthusiasm for its new Muse AI models
  • The Late Earnings Report Index (LERI) sits at 56, well below the 100 baseline, signaling strong corporate clarity for an eighth straight quarter
  • Over 1,000 global companies (including 79 S&P 500 members) are scheduled to report this week as earnings broaden beyond the financial sector

The third-quarter earnings season kicked off with a divergent performance across Wall Street, anchored by an unexpected double miss on both top and bottom lines from JPMorgan Chase.1 

High bond yields severely muted fixed income trading across commercial giants like JPMorgan, Wells Fargo2, and Bank of America3. Conversely, equity trading desks and investment banking dealmaking at firms like Goldman Sachs4 and Morgan Stanley5 provided strong bright spots.

Ultimately, the early bank results highlighted a stark split: while high rates pressured fixed-income desks and funding costs, returning corporate dealmaking provided a critical growth engine.

This week, the focus expands to a broader swath of sectors, ranging from tech and industrials to consumer discretionary and energy, with 79 S&P 500 companies scheduled to report. Early results remain overwhelmingly positive: according to FactSet, of the 9% of S&P 500 companies that have reported so far, 84% have beaten EPS expectations, while 67% have topped revenue estimates. That early performance brings the blended Q3 EPS growth rate to 29.0%, a slight dip from last week but still positioning the index for potentially its third consecutive quarter of earnings growth above 25%.6

A Bullish Schedule Shift? Meta Sets Early Q3 Call Amid AI Agent Breakthroughs 

All eyes are now turning to Meta Platforms (META), which is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Wednesday, October 21. This release date marks Meta’s earliest Q3 report in a decade, arriving seven days ahead of our consensus (October 28) and pulling the tech giant out of the typical “Mega-Cap Tech Week” alongside Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, and Alphabet. It’s also pretty rare to see a company of this size move their earnings date so drastically, in either direction.

Historically, moving an earnings announcement forward is a distinctly bullish signal for investors. Academic research out of MIT and the University of Texas shows that when a company moves up its earnings release relative to historical norms, it strongly correlates with positive news being shared on the earnings call, whereas delayed reports often signal incoming bad news.7 By breaking away from its Big Tech peers to report early, Meta may subtly be signaling confidence to the market. 

Ahead of its early earnings call, Meta’s stock took a slight downturn, falling nearly 3% last week in sympathy with the broader AI selloff. Year-to-date however the stock has shown strong upward momentum, up nearly 10% and within $10 of the all-time high seen in August 2025 ($786.80). Investor enthusiasm has been driven largely by the rollout of its new Muse AI models, leading analysts like Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. to argue that Meta may now be leading the AI race. In a recent note to clients, Ives highlighted Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, emphasizing that breakthrough features like active memory and active focus allow the models to retain context and solve complex, multi-step problems autonomously. These capabilities mark a pivotal shift from simple Q&A tools toward true AI agents capable of handling sustained commercial assignments. Crucially, Meta holds a massive distribution advantage over competitors with 3.6 billion daily active users across its family of apps. By natively integrating these advanced models into existing touchpoints like WhatsApp and Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses, Meta can deploy agentic AI at scale while significantly undercutting user acquisition costs.8

Other Potential Surprises this week

In addition to Meta Platforms, there are three other S&P 500 companies with earlier than usual earnings dates this week. Rollins Inc. is also reporting October 21, a week earlier than the expectation of October 28. Western Digital Corp. will report on October 22, two weeks earlier than our initial estimate of November 5. Lastly, Comcast Inc. will also report on October 22, a week earlier than the forecasted date of October 29, but that is most likely due to the major spin-off taking place which result in two independent publicly traded companies (separating media/entertainment from broadband and wireless). 

CEOs Remain Confident as Q3 Earnings Begin

CEO uncertainty remains low heading into Q3 reports, and in line with the readings from the first three quarters of the year. The Late Earnings Report Index, our proprietary measure of CEO uncertainty, has now recorded eight consecutive quarterly readings below the historical benchmark as companies prepare to report their Q3 results.

The LERI tracks outlier earnings date changes among publicly traded companies with market capitalizations of $250M and higher. The LERI has a baseline reading of 100, and anything above that indicates that companies are feeling uncertain about their current and short-term prospects. A LERI reading under 100 suggests that companies feel they have a pretty good handle on the near-term.

The official pre-peak season LERI reading for Q3 earnings (reported in Q4) stands at 56. This is well below the baseline reading, suggesting when companies announced their earnings dates they were feeling more certain about economic conditions. As of October 14, there were 37 late outliers and 60 early outliers.

Q3 2026 Earnings Wave 

The peak weeks of the Q3 earnings season are expected to fall between October 26 – November 13, with each week expected to see over 2,000 reports. Currently, November 5 is predicted to be the most active day with 1,160 companies anticipated to report. Thus far, only 61% of companies have confirmed their earnings date (out of our universe of 11,000+ global names). The remaining dates are estimated based on historical reporting data.

data.title: Bank of America Stock Breaks Key Trend Line: Could Ending Diagonal Mark A Top?
data.description:
BAC’s post-earnings drop below its April 2025 trend line fits an Elliott Wave ending diagonal and may be the start of a bigger correction.

Bank of America has had a rough few days. After a hefty regulatory penalty and a third-quarter report that fell short of expectations, the stock fell to its lowest level since May. More importantly from my point of view, it broke below the trend line connected from the April 2025 lows.

When a support line that old gives way, I pay attention. From an Elliott Wave perspective, the picture fits a pattern I respect a lot: an ending diagonal.

Looking at the subdivisions of the whole move from the 2024 lows, I can see the shape of a wedge, and the strong drop below it makes me think that pattern may now be completed. If so, an important top could be in place.

Bank of America (BAC) daily chart: the break below the April 2025 trend line, the possible ending diagonal from the 2024 lows, the $53–$57 resistance area on a rebound and $46 as the next major support.

The earnings backdrop

According to the bank’s own results release, Bank of America earned $6.9 billion, or $0.91 per share, in the third quarter, down from $8.3 billion, or $1.04, a year earlier. That includes a $1.2 billion regulatory settlement charge, worth 17 cents per share. Excluding it, adjusted earnings were $1.08 per share, which, according to Reuters, missed the $1.10 analysts expected. Revenue rose 3% to $30.0 billion and net interest income grew 8%, but investment banking fees fell 11% to $1.8 billion and sales and trading revenue slipped 5% to $5.1 billion, as fixed income trading dropped 17% while equities rose 11%.

The penalty, according to Reuters, relates to the bank’s failure to report more than $5 billion in suspicious activity to the US government. The stock fell about 4.8% on Wednesday to close at $51.39, after trading at its lowest since May during the session. The capital position remains solid, with a CET1 ratio of 10.9% and book value of $39.26 per share. By my own calculation, at around $52 the stock trades at roughly 1.3 times book value and 1.8 times tangible book value, and the latest quarterly dividend of 32 cents works out to a yield of about 2.5%.

What is an ending diagonal?

An ending diagonal is a wedge-shaped pattern that usually shows up in the final wave of a trend. Its waves overlap, and each of the five waves tends to unfold in three smaller waves (3-3-3-3-3), which is why the advance often looks tired and choppy rather than powerful. It tells me momentum is fading. When the wedge breaks, the market often reverses sharply, because the move that built the pattern has run out of steam.That is why the trend line break matters here. It is the first sign that buyers have lost control. What I want to see next is a rebound that fails in the $53–$57 area, where the broken trend line and former support should now act as resistance.

Elliott wave ending diagonal: waves 1-2-3-4-5 move within two converging trend lines and complete wave (5).

What I am watching

The stock closed around $51.40 last week, so it sits just under the $53–$57 resistance area and roughly 10% above the next major support at $46. I think we are still only in the first leg of a higher-degree correction, so after some rallies, even back toward the broken trend line, I expect more weakness as long as BAC trades below the $65.45 high.

Of course, nothing is certain. Rallies can be sharp, especially after a big drop, and a move above $65.45 would invalidate this bearish count. Until then, I am treating bounces as opportunities to watch rather than a reason to turn bullish.

Highlights:

  • Bank of America broke below the trend line connected from the April 2025 lows, a dangerous signal.
  • The subdivisions from the 2024 lows suggest an ending diagonal that may now be completed.
  • A rebound toward the broken trend line and the $53–$57 area could still happen.
  • $46 is the next major support.
  • The bearish view remains valid while BAC trades below $65.45.

data.title: META Stock Breaks Out of Triangle: Elliott Wave Points to New Highs
data.description:
Meta is doing pretty well, and not only that, it has outperformed its own sector by more than 20% over the last two months or so.

It has also outperformed the S&P 500 by more than 17%, which is quite impressive, especially if we consider that the communication services sector has been lagging a bit, although not as much as some other sectors like industrials, materials, and financials. Of course, energy and technology are in a league of their own this year.

But overall, if the communication services sector also starts to pick up, then we can expect Meta, which is already performing very well, to extend even higher.

Meta vs sector and S&P 500 relative strength

In fact, looking at this stock from an Elliott Wave perspective, we can see that the price has broken out of the recent triangle, which looks like it could be completed. Price recovered towards $700, and we saw a very sharp and strong recovery. So after some pullback, which could already be playing out now, we could see even more gains. What I would be looking for is support around $692, the previous breakout point. If more aggressive selling occurs in the near term, then $712 is also an important level to watch, as it marks an unfilled gap from mid-September.

Meta daily Elliott Wave chart

So it’s very possible that we will see another push higher in the next few weeks, but who knows, maybe we will have to wait until the next earnings release, scheduled for Wednesday, October 28. Overall, this looks like a bullish, constructive pattern, and new highs could still be coming in wave five, closer to $850, maybe even $900, as long as the market trades above the $500 level.

Highlights:

  • Meta outperforming its sector by more than 20% and the S&P 500 by over 17% in the last two months
  • Elliott Wave triangle appears completed, with a strong bullish breakout
  • Watching support near $692 and the mid-September gap around $712
  • Next earnings release scheduled for October 28
  • Potential wave five targets around $850–900
  • Bullish outlook remains valid above $500

data.title: October Stock Market Surprises? Here’s What To Watch Into Earnings Season
data.description:
• The macro is in focus through month-end, but investors must not overlook company-level trends in the days ahead, including an active conference circuit
  • Stocks remain resilient despite higher Treasury rates and Fed hiking, with the S&P 500 near record highs, led by tech
  • Jobs data, consumer spending, and corporate guidance will be key signals as investors eye Q4 volatility catalysts and 2027 forecasts

It’s really starting to feel like autumn now. August PPI, CPI, and Retail Sales are in the books, the September FOMC meeting is out of the way, and we can now look forward to Jobs Week on Wall Street. Football is in full swing, and earnings season begins before you know it, with Pepsi (PEP) posting results on Thursday, October 8, followed the next morning by Delta (DAL). 

Tuesday, October 13, is the Super Bowl for the Financials sector. That’s when JPMorgan Chase (JPM), Wells Fargo (WFC), Citigroup (C), and Goldman Sachs (GS) report July through September numbers. Bank of America (BAC) and Morgan Stanley (MS) then report on Wednesday, October 14. Before the Q3 earnings deluge, keep your eye on Costco (COST) this Thursday evening.

Earnings Have Been a Treat

Will there be a slew of October surprises in store from corporate America? Hard to say, but if the recent trend holds, it might not be all that spooky. Consider that the S&P 500 reported earnings growth of more than 50% YoY in Q2, the best growth rate in five years, according to John Butters at FactSet. Profits were driven by operations, for sure, but several seemingly one-time factors supported the EPS surge. 

For instance, “other income” related to gains on private investments helped the Information Technology sector, soaring oil prices fueled Energy-sector earnings, tariff refunds aided consumer areas, not to mention intense AI-powered capex feeding directly to the bottom lines of semiconductor companies.

Inflation is Tricky

AI players have also been active on the debt-issuance front. Partly for that reason, the Fed hiked rates on September 16. The move wasn’t unexpected, but it didn’t come without a dose of controversy. Some macro pundits assert that the current 3.7% PCE Price Index inflation rate will naturally cool, given subsiding effects of tariffs, the conflict in Iran, summertime software price spikes, and questionable recording of portfolio management cost increases. More hawkish Wall Street economists underscore that at some point, a series of “one-off” factors can no longer be framed as a temporary phenomenon, and that a new macro-volatility backdrop is upon us.

What does the market say? Perhaps some central bank tightening is workable. Consider that the 2-year Treasury yield has come within a quarter point of 5%, and the Fed Funds futures market prices in three more hikes by Q3 2027. It’s as if the market relays to the FOMC that taking back the three insurance cuts executed over the final four months of 2025 would not be a policy mistake.

US CPI Inflation Rose to +0.4% in August

Tech Stocks Are Powering Markets Again, Leaving Some Cyclicals Behind

Another indicator? Stock prices. The S&P 500 is within a percentage point of its August 14 all-time high. The Nasdaq 100 may have broken out from its Q3 downtrend. International indexes are knocking on new highs. While breadth could be better (the Mag 7 is leading once again), equities appear to have no problem with higher borrowing costs. 

It’s not all roses, however, with cyclical sectors like Industrials, Consumer Discretionary (ex-Amazon and Tesla), and areas of Financials still well off their 2026 highs. U.S. small- and mid-cap stocks didn’t exactly have a banner summer, either.

Main Street Feels the Squeeze, Though the “K” May be Closing

Further Fed tightening could do additional damage to indebted households, too. According to Econoday, the most recent University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers revealed a top-five weakest sentiment reading. Stubbornly high gas prices and soaring diesel sting Main Street, with higher energy costs likely to seep into what we all pay at the grocery store by the time the holidays roll around.

University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment Fell Again in September

“UMich” has been ugly, but official August Retail Sales numbers put out by the U.S. Census Bureau were downright gaudy. The key back-to-school shopping season appeared to be a strong one, even backing out gasoline expenditures. Online spending, electronics & appliances, sporting goods, and even restaurant activity were impressive. 

The top half of income earners always carries the bulk of the load, but, as some BofA card-spending data show, the “K-shaped” economy has normalized since the start of 2026. The bottom 50% of the workforce has seen improved wage growth, and they have stepped up their discretionary spending.

US Retail Sales Surged 1.2% in August

Gaming Out 2027

All of this leads into the Q4 conference season, when investors get their first look at CY 2027 forecasts from the world’s most important companies. Executives have weathered many macro storms since 2020, and today’s challenges come with just as many opportunities. New technologies, global growth, and strong capital markets could result in bold projects and long-term investments. Our team will keep tabs on the latest developments over the coming weeks. 

The Bottom Line

Following major August data and the September Fed meeting, traders get a chance to catch their breath ahead of the Q3 earnings season. Jobs data starts rolling in Wednesday next week, with the November midterm elections coming closer into view. While eyes are on the macro, investors must heed guidance from the corporate world on their plans for the year ahead.

data.title: AMD Elliott Wave: Tracking a Complex Wave Four Pullback
data.description:
AMD (Advanced Micro Devices) slowed down recently after we identified five waves up with an extended wave three, so we are now tracking a wave four pullback. We think this correction could become a bit more complex and longer in time — especially when we compare it with wave two of the same degree.

In Elliott Wave Theory, fourth waves often take more time and develop more sideways or overlapping structure than second waves.

That is why patience matters here: the 38.2% or even the 50% retracement can still be retested, particularly if we consider the open gap around the 360–394 area.

If you are looking to join the broader uptrend later, that support zone is a much better place to watch for potential rebound opportunities — while the bullish structure remains valid with AMD trading above the 267 invalidation level.

Quick reminder: in a five-wave impulse, wave four is the corrective pause after a strong wave three. It should not break the end of wave one (here reflected by the 267 invalidation).

Until that level holds, the larger count still points to a later wave five advance once wave four completes. For more analysis visit us at wavetraders.com and apply for 7 day free access.

data.title: Dividends and Buybacks Slump as Macro Risks Mount in Q3
data.description:
• Dividend reductions hit 19% of total announcements thus far in Q3 2026, the highest proportion of dividend cuts since the peak of Covid-19 in Q2 2020
  • Buyback volume seems to be trending lower with only 91 authorizations tracked so far, pacing toward a 10-year historic low
  • Massive AI infrastructure capital commitments, escalating Middle East conflicts, and tariff pressures force C-suites into cash-preservation mode

The Main Line of Defense Begins to Falter

For decades, equity investors have relied on a foundational promise from Corporate America: the continuous return of surplus cash. Dividends and share repurchases represent the two primary ways by which companies deliver tangible value back to shareholders. Yet as we navigate the final stretch of the third quarter of 2026, both channels are signaling a distinct shift toward restraint. Rather than expanding payouts in tandem with market valuations, boardrooms across sectors are quietly tapping the brakes on capital returns. 

Understanding this pivot requires stepping back to how these two mechanisms operate within corporate strategy. Dividends serve as the direct, cash-in-hand reward, a regular commitment of capital that signals stable cash flows and balance sheet strength.

Share buybacks, on the other hand, act as a dynamic flexible valve: by reducing total outstanding shares, they boost earnings per share (EPS) and signal management’s belief that their stock is undervalued. Together, they constitute the lifeblood of total shareholder yield. When both mechanisms trend downward simultaneously, it provides a potential signal that management teams are either prioritizing cash preservation over short-term distribution, or using that cash for something else.

Dividend Decreases Reach Post-Pandemic Highs

With only two weeks left in the third quarter, the dividend landscape paints a sobering picture. Among companies issuing payout announcements so far in Q3 2026, a striking 19% have declared dividend reductions from prior levels. To put this in perspective, this represents the highest percentage of dividend decreases observed in a single quarter since Q2 2020’s 21%, when the global economy was paralyzed by the Covid-19 pandemic. Unlike that time, there have not been any dividend suspensions in Q3.

Buybacks Pace Toward a Decade Low

The pull-back is even more pronounced when examining share repurchase activity. Buyback announcements currently stand at just 91 for Q3 2026 (as of September 14, 2026). If activity stays around this level through month-end, it will mark the lowest single-quarter buyback count in the entire 10-year history of this dataset.

To contextualize how subdued this activity is, the next lowest number of buyback announcements was seen in Q3 2022 at 112 authorizations, a period marked by heavy Fed tightening and heightened recession fears. Falling below that benchmark underscores a broad institutional reluctance to commit balance sheet reserves to stock repurchases in the current environment.

What is Gobbling Up Corporate Cash?

Why are executives pulling back on shareholder returns precisely when equity markets demand strong fundamentals? Two primary forces are likely driving this capital reallocation: 

First, cash is being consumed by the relentless AI build-out. Aggressive capital expenditure commitments are no longer limited to megacap tech giants; companies across industrials, energy, logistics, and corporate services are sinking substantial capital into AI infrastructure, software integrations, and power grid upgrades just to remain competitive. Cash that previously funded discretionary repurchases is now earmarked for multi-year technology builds. 

Second, macro uncertainty and geopolitical tensions are forcing CFOs to build protective cash cushions. Worries over tariff costs and surging oil prices stemming from the Iran war have pushed risk management to the forefront. Combined with persistent input inflation, corporate treasury desks may be prioritizing liquidity over payouts. 

The Bottom Line

It is easy for investors to stay fixated on daily market fluctuations and high-level macroeconomic headlines. However, corporate capital allocation decisions often reveal the true temperature of executive sentiment. The simultaneous spike in dividend cuts and historical drop in buyback authorizations signal that management teams are shifting toward balance sheet defense and long-term capital investments over immediate payouts. As quarter-end approaches, monitoring these capital return trends will be vital for understanding how Corporate America views the road ahead.

data.title: From Apple to NVIDIA: Big Tech’s Volatility Calendar Is Loaded
data.description:
• Post-Labor Day vol heats up, with Treasury yields, crude oil, and agricultural commodities steering the S&P 500
  • Apple’s iPhone 18 event takes center stage this week, while NVIDIA and other semiconductor heavyweights headline a packed Goldman Sachs tech conference
  • The catalyst calendar is packed through September, with NVIDIA events, CRM Dreamforce and Meta Connect all on tap

It’s time to stash away your summer gear. An active corporate event stretch is upon us. The post-Labor Day trade is often rife with volatility, and we’ve already seen some fireworks across asset classes.

To kick off the holiday-shortened week, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield scaled 4.80%, potentially pacing for its highest weekly print since October 2023. Global crude oil, as measured by the prompt Brent contract, is within earshot of $100 for the first time since May. All the while, geopolitical strife and even Mother Nature (thanks to El Niño) upset supply-demand balances for agricultural commodities worldwide.

The Stage is Yours, John

Big tech has its own slate of volatility sparks on tap. Following last week’s Tesla (TSLA) whimper of a stock price response to its Cybercab Austin, TX, rollout, eyes now turn to Apple (AAPL). It’s rookie CEO John Ternus’s big scene, as he and the team unveil the latest iPhone. Apple Event 2026 is expected to center on iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. The world’s second-most valuable company may also step into the foldable phone arena, with a rumored model called the iPhone Ultra. We’ll learn all the specifics starting at 1 p.m. ET Wednesday, and the “Surprise and Shine” keynote streams live from Cupertino. 

Should traders anticipate fireworks? Maybe not. According to data from Option Research & Technology Services, shares trade with a tame 26% implied volatility, which broadly equates to a 1.6% daily stock price change. What’s more, AAPL has just a 33% positive rate on Event Days, so says analytics firm Bluekurtic Market Insights. Whether this week’s event proves to be another ‘sell the news’ opportunity remains to be seen. 

A further decline off its July 29 record high of $344 would be understandable, given the rapid recovery from the $245 March nadir. AAPL is up almost 17% on the year, dividends included, so the bulls are satisfied, but Ternus has a lot to live up to after a 2700% total return over former CEO Tim Cook’s tenure. 

NVIDIA & Jensen Wait in the Wings

“Surprise and Shine” will have analysts’ attention mid-week. Meanwhile, one of the biggest and potentially market-moving tech gatherings is ongoing just 42 miles north of the Apple shindig.  

The Goldman Sachs Communacopia Technology Conference 2026 features several high-profile hardware, software, and cybersecurity stalwarts, none more prominent than NVIDIA (NVDA). Its management team is slated to speak Thursday at 11:50 a.m. ET, according to Wall Street Horizon’s event data, though that is still pending confirmation. Global semiconductor names such as ASML (ASML), AMD (AMD), KLA Corp (KLAC), and Broadcom (AVGO), among others, are on hand. 

Also in attendance at Goldman’s gathering are Mag 7 members Alphabet (GOOGL) and Microsoft (MSFT). It’s not a one-sector show, either, as Walmart (WMT) and Mastercard (MA) may provide details on tech with respect to consumer impacts. Investors can expect to hear updates from the digital security industry as well, with CrowdStrike (CRWD) and Palo Alto Networks (PANW) on hand. 

NVIDIA’s 70% Question

Once the Apple fanfare winds down, NVIDIA could grab the spotlight, depending on what’s said at the IBC 2026 Conference this Friday. The event spills over into Fed Week, and it’s possible that the company’s ambitious FY 2028 sales growth rate of 70% could receive more color. If not this week, the firm could provide details later in September at All In 2026 (the 16th) and its NVIDIA AI Day Singapore 2026 (the 22nd). 

Lastly, NVIDIA presents at the Experience POWER Conference 2026 the same day as Microsoft, on the final Monday of the third quarter. 

Earnings Season Is on the Horizon

Gazing ahead to the Q3 reporting season, Tesla gets things going with its unconfirmed October 21 earnings date, followed a week later by Alphabet, Meta Platforms (META), and Microsoft. Apple and Amazon have unconfirmed reports on October 29, with nearly $2 trillion market cap SpaceX (SPCX) posting results likely on Election Day in the U.S. (Tuesday, November 3).  

Here’s a trick to help keep them straight: M&M Wednesday, A&A Thursday is usually how it goes (meaning, Meta & Microsoft come before Apple & Amazon). With such a busy corporate event calendar, we should take all the mnemonics we can get!

Software & AI Together at Last?

Volatility might also be stirred as the Fed convenes next week. Salesforce (CRM) hosts its annual Dreamforce event, also in the City by the Bay. After CEO Marc Benioff locked arms with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last month following CRM’s earnings report, a new twist emerges in the AI story: maybe AI won’t be eating software, after all.

Always the showman, but also one of the best tech chiefs around, Benioff could unveil new partnerships. Perhaps a fresh autumnal catalyst is, in fact, needed, given CRM’s massive $146 to $268 summer rally. The Dow component has shed 6% between since last Thursday’s close, though.

Driving the Social Media Narrative

Wrapping things up, Meta Connect happens September 23-24. This corporate confab is marketed to home in on the hyperscaler’s AI technologies, AI glasses, and VR. Mark Zuckerberg and team surely hope to direct media attention away from recent regulatory headlines and settlement figures.

Shares are down 6% on the year, even after a five-day winning streak through this past Tuesday afternoon. Investors are no doubt frustrated by a steady diet of lower highs on the chart, while $520 has attracted buyers on a pair of occasions in 2026.

The Bottom Line

Portfolio managers and analysts are back from holiday, and we are hitting the ground running. Apple’s iPhone event hopes to buck bearish stock reaction trends, while the broader Goldman Sachs tech conference may offer clues on the latest hardware and AI breakthroughs. NVIDIA is on the road all month, and earnings season will be here before you know it. Through it all, keep up with Wall Street Horizon for all the macro and micro volatility catalysts.
